slides.title: A promise instead of memory
slides.main: malloc hands out addresses, and frames are allocated on first access.

captions: The program calls malloc and gets a pointer
The addresses are handed out, but there is no real memory behind them yet
The first access causes a page fault
The kernel allocates a frame and records it in the page table

frames.text: addresses handed out, no frames behind them
the kernel allocated a frame and recorded it in the table

slides.title: Pages and folios
slides.main: The kernel thinks in 4 KiB pages and, more and more, in folios.

captions: Physical memory is divided into four-kilobyte pages
A page may belong to a program, to a file cache, or be free
For each one the kernel keeps an owner, a reference count and flags
A folio combines several pages into one unit of accounting

frames.text: memory is cut into 4 KiB pages
for each page: owner, reference count, flags
a folio is several pages managed as one

slides.title: Zones and nodes
slides.sub: Not all memory is the same
slides.main: The kernel accounts for device limits and the nearest memory node.

captions: Physical addresses are divided into zones: low, middle and normal
Old devices reach only the low zone, and the kernel accounts for that
On multi-socket machines, memory nodes are added
When allocating a page, the kernel prefers the nearest node

frames.text: the kernel takes a page from the nearest node

slides.title: Buddy system
slides.main: Blocks split in half and merge back — that fights fragmentation.

captions: Free memory is kept in blocks of 2 to the order pages
Need a smaller block: split a big one into buddies
One buddy is given away, the rest stay on the free lists
Freed buddies merge: a fight against fragmentation

frames.text: need 2: split in half until it fits
hand out 2, the other buddies stay free

slides.title: Slab and kmalloc
slides.main: Caches of identical cells give objects in a few cycles.

captions: A whole page for a small kernel object is too wasteful
SLUB cuts pages into identical cells for one object type
Handout — take a free cell from the list in a few cycles
The list of caches and their size is visible in slabtop; kmalloc is built the same way

frames.text: a whole page for one object — wasteful

slides.title: Address space
slides.main: A process is a set of regions; they are kept in a maple tree since kernel 6.1.

captions: The address space is a set of regions: code, data, heap, libraries, stack
Each region is described by an entry with bounds and permissions; it is visible in maps
Regions are kept in a tree; since kernel 6.1 it is a maple tree
Addresses are randomized on every start — this makes an attack harder

slides.title: Page fault
slides.main: A minor fault needs no disk, a major one reads from it.

captions: The program touches a page that is not in the table yet
The processor finds no entry and calls the fault handler
The kernel checks the region, takes a frame, zeroes it and records it in the table
The instruction is retried; the fault is minor without disk and major with a read

frames.text: the instruction touched an unmapped page
the processor found no entry and called the kernel
the kernel checks the region and allocates a zeroed frame

slides.title: Page tables
slides.main: The TLB hides the table walk, huge pages shorten it.

captions: A virtual address splits into level indexes and an offset
By the indexes the kernel and processor walk four tables to the frame
The TLB caches finished translations and lets the walk be skipped
A 2 MiB huge page makes the chain shorter and the TLB more effective

frames.text: the address is cut into indexes: 9 bits per level and a 12-bit offset
four table reads on every access — expensive
huge page 2 MiB: the chain is one level shorter

slides.title: Reclaim and swap
slides.main: MGLRU evicts the oldest generation; swap may also be in compressed memory.

captions: MGLRU sorts pages into generations: from new to the oldest
When free pages run low, the kswapd reclaim thread wakes up
The oldest generation goes: file cache is dropped, anonymous pages go to swap
Swap can be kept on disk or in compressed memory

frames.text: kswapd woke up: few free pages

slides.title: OOM and limits
slides.sub: When there is no memory at all
slides.main: cgroup limits and systemd-oomd keep trouble from reaching the whole machine.

captions: No free pages, nothing to evict
The OOM killer computes a score for each process; oom_score_adj protects the important
The process with the highest score gets SIGKILL
cgroup limits contain the trouble, and systemd-oomd watches pressure ahead of time

frames.text: oom_score: the more memory held, the higher the score
the victim is the biggest: gets SIGKILL
group limit: the kill happens only inside it; systemd-oomd reacts earlier
